visits.text: Leave Latacunga for Quilotoa Lagoon, roughly 2h west through Andean farmland. Quilotoa is a volcano whose last confirmed eruption dates to 1280. It left behind a 3-km-diameter, 250-m-deep crater filled with turquoise water that shifts color with the light. At 3,914 m elevation, it's one of Ecuador's most photogenic sites. From the crater rim, the view is striking. Descend to the lake if you've got energy—30 min down steep, but the climb back (40-50 min) is taxing at this altitude. For the weary, mules are available for the ascent.

The Waterfall Route (Ruta de las Cascadas) is Baños' star attraction: nearly 20 km toward Puyo, with some sixty waterfalls along the Río Pastaza valley. Rent a bike—the road is almost entirely downhill. First stop: Manto de la Novia cascade ("Bridal Veil"), which you can fly over via tarabita above the gorge. Continue to Río Verde and Pailón del Diablo ("Devil's Cauldron")—80 meters high, a force that soaks you in 30 seconds up close. Passages carved through rock let you slip behind the cascade. It's one of South America's most impressive waterfalls.

Heading back up to Baños, stop at Casa del Arbol, a former Tungurahua volcano observation post turned attraction. Its famous swing suspended over the void at 2,660 m delivers vertigo-inducing photos with the volcano backdrop—if weather cooperates. The site is small, count 30 minutes.

activities.text: After Quilotoa, drive toward Baños de Agua Santa (3-4h). You descend from the high plateaus into the Río Pastaza valley, dropping from 3,900 m to 1,815 m—the climate warms noticeably and vegetation turns tropical. Arriving in Baños, loop the central square to see the Basílica de la Virgen de Agua Santa, a pilgrimage site where frescoes depict miracles attributed to the Virgin. Then climb to the Bellavista viewpoint for your first glimpse of the town dominated by Tungurahua volcano (5,023 m), active since 1999.

Bike the waterfall route from Baños to Río Verde. The descent is easy and landscapes shift from Andean mountain to tropical vegetation. On return, local pickup trucks load bikes and cyclists to haul everyone back to Baños—very handy.

Late afternoon, unwind in Baños' thermal baths. The hot, sulfurous waters flow directly from Tungurahua volcano. Several pools at varying temperatures (18 to 54°C). The local specialty to try on your way out: melcocha, a sugarcane candy stretched by hand right in front of you.

visits.text: Long driving day (4-5h) between Riobamba and Cuenca, but the detour through Ingapirca makes it fascinating. At 3,160 meters elevation, you'll discover Ecuador's most important archaeological site. First occupied by the Cañari people from around 500 AD, then conquered by the Incas around 1487, it features an elliptical Temple of the Sun—unique in the entire known Inca world. The diorite stones are assembled without mortar with surgical precision. Charles Marie de La Condamine was the first European to describe it in 1739.

The guided tour (mandatory, included in the ticket) lasts about 40 minutes and covers the Temple of the Sun, agricultural terraces, and a natural rock whose shape evokes an Inca face. The museum inaugurated in 2018 displays ceramics, textiles, and tools from both civilizations. Don't expect Machu Picchu—the site is modest in size—but the story of Cañari-Inca fusion is captivating. If you have energy, a 30-minute trail descends into the Intihuayco valley.

Arrive in Cuenca by late afternoon. Detour through the Turi viewpoint on the hill south of the city. From there, you'll have the best panoramic view of Cuenca and its sky-blue domes—the evening light brings out the red tile roofs and bell towers. It's the perfect postcard to open your Cuenca stay.

Start at Parque Calderón, the city's heart, and the Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepción that overlooks it. Its blue domes are Cuenca's symbol—visible from everywhere. Begun in 1885 and completed only in 1975, it was supposed to have two additional towers topped with cupolas, but the architect had to abandon the plan: the ground couldn't support more weight. The interior floors are Carrara marble imported from Italy. Climb the 155 steps to the domes for a plunging view over the historic center.

Across the way, don't miss the Catedral Vieja (El Sagrario), one of Latin America's oldest churches, built in 1557. Now transformed into a religious art museum, it surprises with its pastel ceiling paintings—very different from the typical gilded church interiors. Entrance is free.

Two blocks from the cathedral, the Plaza de las Flores is enchanting. The permanent flower market, run by women in traditional dress, overflows with roses, lilies, and orchids—Ecuador is one of the world's largest flower exporters. The white Carmen de la Asunción church (1730) forms a dazzling backdrop. This plaza was voted one of the world's most beautiful flower markets.

Walk down to the Pumapungo Museum, built on the ruins of the ancient Inca city of Tomebamba—"the Puma's Gate." The open-air archaeological site shows remnants of an Inca administrative center, and the adjoining botanical garden presents over 200 native Andean plants. The indoor museum covers Ecuador's ethnographic history and indigenous cultures. Free admission.

Day trip to Cajas National Park, just 40 minutes from Cuenca toward Guayaquil. This 28,544-hectare park, created in 1977 and designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve, holds over 230 lakes of glacial origin between 3,100 and 4,450 meters elevation. The páramo landscapes—these high grassy moorlands—recall Scotland on an overcast day. A remnant of the Inca Trail crosses the park for 4 km between Luspa cave and Mamamag lake. Entrance is free but registration with passport is mandatory.

For an accessible hike, do the loop around Laguna Toreadora (trail #1, 2.2 km, ~1h30) from the visitor center. If you're in shape and acclimatized, climb toward the Lagunas Unidas on trail #4 (4.2 km) which crosses a polylepis forest—these twisted trees grow higher than any other tree on Earth. The lakes follow one another in total silence, broken only by birds. Bring warm, waterproof clothing: weather changes fast at this altitude.

activities.text: Enjoy the evening for a first meal in this city renowned for its Andean gastronomy. Mote pillo (white corn sautéed with eggs and onions) is the local specialty. The small restaurants around the market are the best. Cuenca is very pleasant on foot in the evening, the pedestrian streets are well-lit and the atmosphere is much calmer than Quito.

Late in the day, walk down Calle Larga to the Barranco neighborhood along the Tomebamba River. The colorful facades overlooking the river form one of Ecuador's most photographed landscapes. Take the opportunity to visit a Panama hat workshop—here they call them "sombrero de paja toquilla." The Cuenca region is the heart of this artisan production inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. A good hat takes weeks of weaving.

On the return from the hike, stop at the Tres Cruces viewpoint, the highest point on the Cuenca-Guayaquil road (4,167 m). On clear days, you can see the Pacific coast from this point—it's the only place in Ecuador where both slopes are visible simultaneously. Back in Cuenca, rest your legs in the Baños de Cuenca hot springs (8 km from downtown), fed by volcanic sources. Hot water at this altitude is pure luxury.

visits.text: Drive from Cuenca to Guayaquil (about 4h), a spectacular 2,500-meter descent from altitude to sea level. You'll pass through Cajas park (quick view if you skipped it yesterday) then cross banana and cacao plantations as you approach the coast. The tropical heat will hit you all at once—prepare for thermal shock after the Andes.

Arriving in Guayaquil, head straight to the Las Peñas neighborhood, the city's oldest. Climb the 444 steps of Cerro Santa Ana through the brightly painted facades—each landing bears a number and an anecdote. At the top, the lighthouse and small chapel offer a panoramic view over the Guayas River, the Malecón, and the city rooftops. Go in late afternoon for the golden light and the atmosphere of the bars and art galleries lining the stairs.

Walk down to the Malecón 2000, the 2.5-km promenade along the Guayas River. Renovated in the early 2000s, it connects the artisan market in the south to the Las Peñas neighborhood in the north. You'll find gardens, fountains, monuments, and Parque Seminario—don't miss it: its trees are populated by land iguanas basking in the sun by the dozens. Kids love them, but keep your distance: they can bite.

Drive from Montañita to Guayaquil (about 3h). Arriving, start with Parque Seminario (also called Parque de las Iguanas), right downtown. Dozens of land iguanas lounge in the trees and on the lawns—a surreal spectacle in the middle of a big city. Guayaquil's neo-Gothic cathedral borders the park. Grab a bench to watch local life between the giant lizards.

Continue to the Mercado Artesanal, Guayaquil's largest craft market. You'll find Panama hats, hammocks, tagua jewelry (vegetable ivory), and Andean textiles. Vendors are open to bargaining—but stay reasonable. The market is covered, which is appreciated when Guayaquil's heat hits hard.

If you didn't climb Cerro Santa Ana on your first pass (D8), now's the time. Otherwise, explore the Barrio del Astillero, a neighborhood in transformation that preserves 19th-century wooden houses. This neighborhood, the city's old shipyard, is less touristy than Las Peñas and gives a more authentic glimpse of working-class Guayaquil.

Start with the MAAC (Museo Antropológico y de Arte Contemporáneo), located at the southern end of Malecón 2000. This free museum displays a collection of over 50,000 archaeological pieces tracing 5,000 years of Ecuadorian cultures, from the Valdivia civilization (South America's oldest ceramic culture) through the colonial era. The contemporary art section is also worth a look.

If you still have a morning, cross the pedestrian bridge to Isla Santay, a nature reserve in the middle of the Guayas River. This mangrove island is accessible for free and offers 2 km of boardwalk trails over the water. You'll encounter herons, iguanas, and mangrove crabs. It's a surprising nature break just a few hundred meters from downtown.

activities.text: Evening on the Malecón: the riverside restaurants serve shrimp ceviche (Guayaquil's specialty) and encebollado, a tuna and onion soup considered the country's best hangover cure. The nighttime atmosphere is lively, especially on weekends.

End of day on the Malecón del Estero Salado, less known than Malecón 2000 but just as pleasant. This promenade follows an arm of sea bordered by mangroves right in the city center. Boats offer short sunset rides on the water. The atmosphere is more local and less touristy than the main Malecón.

Final stop before departure: the Parque Histórico de Guayaquil, located in Samborondón (20 minutes by taxi). This park-museum reconstructs 19th-century coastal architecture and houses animals in a restored mangrove setting. It's a good place to understand the coastal region's history before catching your flight from José Joaquín de Olmedo airport, 10 minutes from downtown.

visits.text: Big driving day: from Mindo, loop back through the foothills of Pichincha then head due south toward Cotopaxi National Park (count 4-5h total). Cotopaxi awaits with its nearly perfect snow-capped cone at 5,897 m—one of the world's highest active volcanoes. Its last major eruption in 1877 sent mudflows that destroyed Latacunga and several valley towns. Pack warm clothes: the park is windy and you'll be above 3,800 m.

Stop at Limpiopungo Lagoon, at 3,800 m elevation at the volcano's foot. On clear days, Cotopaxi's snow-capped cone mirrors in the calm waters—Ecuador's classic postcard shot. The trail loops the lake in 1h to 1h30, easy-going and ideal for spotting Andean ducks, Andean gulls, and—with luck—a carunculated caracara. Walk slowly—altitude makes itself felt.

activities.text: If well-acclimatized, drive up to the parking lot at 4,500 m then hike to the José Rivas refuge at 4,864 m—half an hour of steep climbing through volcanic sand. From the refuge, you can continue 45 min to the glacier edge at 5,000 m. Shortness of breath guaranteed, but the view over the ice cap and Avenue of Volcanoes will take what's left. Grab a hot chocolate at the refuge on your way down.

visits.text: Long drive from Otavalo to Mindo (roughly 4h via Nanegalito). The landscape shifts dramatically: you leave the dry highlands and plunge into the Andean cloud forest of the Chocó bioregion at 1,250 m elevation. Mindo is a former farming village turned naturalist's paradise—Birdlife International designated it an Important Bird Area. Ecuador harbors 130 of the world's 340 hummingbird species, and many live here. On arrival, take advantage of feeders at your lodging to observe these colorful rockets.

Head to the Mariposario, 2.5 km from the center. Under a massive glass greenhouse, over 1,000 butterflies of 25 species fly freely around you. Place a piece of banana on your fingers—they'll come feed on it. With luck, you'll witness a butterfly emerging from its chrysalis. At the entrance feeders, hummingbirds put on a constant show.

activities.text: Take the tarabita (metal gondola suspended from a cable) that crosses the canopy to access the waterfall sanctuary. Three trails: Nambillo cascade (15 min one-way, easy), La Reina cascade (50 min, most impressive), or the 5-waterfall circuit (2h round-trip). Paths are narrow and muddy—bring hiking shoes, rain gear, and a swimsuit if you want to bathe at the falls' base.

Late afternoon, join a chocolate-making workshop. Ecuadorian cacao ("fino de aroma" variety) ranks among the world's finest, and several Mindo producers offer the complete process from bean to bar, tasting included.

visits.text: Coastal drive south (about 1h) to Montañita, Ecuador's most famous surf village. The vibe is radically different from the rest of the trip: this is a concentration of backpackers, surfers, and craft vendors. The main street is pedestrian, lined with bars, ceviche restaurants, and shell jewelry shops. If you're seeking calm, continue 5 km north to Olón beach, much quieter and just as beautiful.

Before settling in Montañita, push 5 km north to Olón. This fishing village is the antithesis of Montañita: calm, family-friendly, with a huge beach nearly deserted on weekdays. On the cliff separating the two villages, the Santuario de Olón—a small white church perched above the ocean—offers a magnificent panorama of the coast. The trail leading there from the beach takes 15 minutes and is worth the detour for photos.

Back in Montañita, the beach offers a long stretch of sand with consistent waves—ideal for surfing. Schools offer lessons for all levels, budget 2h for an introduction. Walking north from the center, a wilder spot at the base of the rocky point attracts locals away from the crowds. If surfing isn't your thing, swimming is pleasant but watch the current—stay in supervised areas.

activities.text: Montañita is mostly known for its nightlife. Bars open in late afternoon with live music, and the party continues until late. If you prefer a more zen plan, sunset from the rocky point north of the beach is superb—bring a local beer and settle in. The shrimp cocktail sold by beach vendors is a classic end-of-day treat.

days_plan.itin_title: Ecuador Road Trip: Volcano Highway, Inca Ruins & Pacific Coast

visits.text: Head north to Otavalo, 95 km from Quito via the Panamericana—count 2 hours with Cayambe and Imbabura volcanoes as your backdrop. On arrival, make straight for Plaza de los Ponchos, South America's most famous artisan market. Its roots stretch back to pre-Columbian times, when the Otavaleños already traded textiles and goods. Open daily, it explodes on Saturdays with hundreds of stalls selling hand-woven ponchos, alpaca wool blankets, silver jewelry, and hammocks. Haggling is expected—it's part of the game. On weekdays, prices are better and the vibe more relaxed.

Loop around Parque Bolívar and Calle Sucre. Otavalo sits at 2,530 m at the foot of Imbabura (4,630 m) and Cotacachi (4,944 m) volcanoes. Otavaleños are recognizable by their long black braids and traditional clothing—a cultural pride remarkably preserved across centuries. If you're here on Saturday, don't miss the livestock market 1 km from the plaza—cows, pigs, chickens, and guinea pigs change hands from 6am onward.

Set out early for Cuicocha Lagoon, 30 minutes from Otavalo. This crater lake formed 3,000 years ago during an eruption of Cotacachi volcano—3 km in diameter, 200 m deep, and two islands shaped like guinea pig backs in the center (hence the Quechua name: "guinea pig lake"). The waters shift from deep blue to emerald green. You can take a boat tour around the islets (25 min) to admire the colors up close.

On the way back, stop at Peguche village, 3 km from Otavalo. Its 18-meter waterfall is sacred to Otavaleños—every June 21st during Inti Raymi (Festival of the Sun), locals come for ritual nocturnal purification baths in the cold water. Outside this period, it's a peaceful walk through eucalyptus forest (20 min). The village specializes in weaving—step into a workshop to watch traditional looms in action.
Passing through Cotacachi, 20 minutes from Otavalo, stop in this small town renowned for leather craftsmanship—jackets, bags, belts, and boots line the main street at very reasonable prices.

activities.text: Late day, swing by San Pablo Lake, 10 km away at the foot of Imbabura volcano. Stop at the El Lechero viewpoint: the millennial tree standing there is a sacred site where indigenous people from across the country come for purification rituals. The 360° view over the lake, volcano, and patchwork farmland is well worth the detour.

Hike the Gorki Campuzano trail around Cuicocha Lagoon: 14 km of ridgeline between 3,100 and 3,500 m elevation, with stunning views over the crater and—on clear days—Imbabura, Cayambe, and Pichincha volcanoes. The trail is marked, rolling but without technical difficulty. Bring water and snacks—there's nothing along the route.

visits.text: After landing at Baltra and taking the bus then ferry to Santa Cruz, you arrive in Puerto Ayora—the Galápagos' most populated settlement with 18,000 residents. Get your bearings along Avenida Charles Darwin. Sea lions are already lounging on the public benches by the dock. Drop your bags and head straight to the Charles Darwin Research Station, a 20-minute walk from the center. Founded in 1959 and opened to the public in 1964, over 150 scientists work here on archipelago conservation. Admission is free—just show your National Park ticket.

Next door is the Fausto Llerena Breeding Center. Since 1965, more than 2,000 giant tortoises have been raised and released here. You'll see hatchlings just 8 cm long alongside adults weighing 250 kg—the scale is staggering. Lonesome George, the last tortoise from Pinta Island who died in 2012 at over 100 years old, rests here in a climate-controlled display. Don't miss the botanical garden with giant endemic daisies (Scalesia affinis). Plan 45 minutes.

Follow with Playa de la Estación, a short walk from the research station. This sheltered sandy beach is the most accessible snorkeling spot from Puerto Ayora—15 minutes on foot from the dock. The water is clear and shallow, perfect for your first encounter with marine iguanas, Sally Lightfoot crabs, and small reef sharks. Bring water shoes for the rocky entry.

If energy remains, walk to Tortuga Bay—allow 30 to 45 minutes from town via a paved trail through Opuntia cacti and palo santo trees. You arrive first at Playa Brava: a long, white-sand shore pounded by surf. Swimming is off-limits, but iguanas rule here. Continue another 20 minutes to Playa Mansa—calm turquoise water where small blacktip sharks cruise the lagoon. Kayak rentals are available. Bring water and snacks; there are no facilities. Return by 6 pm when sea turtles arrive to nest.

Today, head to Santa Cruz's highlands. Hire a taxi from Puerto Ayora (20 minutes; negotiate round-trip rate). First stop: Los Gemelos, two immense sinkholes flanking the main road. Despite their name, these aren't craters—they're collapses of magma chambers. Each spans roughly 300 meters across and 300 meters deep. The surrounding Scalesia forest—Earth's tallest daisy species, found only here—creates a dense canopy. Watch for eight of Darwin's 13 finch species and the vermillion flycatcher. Morning light brings out the birds.

Continue to the El Chato tortoise reserve, 22 km from Puerto Ayora. This 12-hectare private property offers rare, close encounters with wild Chelonoidis porteri giant tortoises in their natural state. Weighing up to 250 kg and measuring 1.5 meters, you'll find them grazing or wallowing in mud. Keep 2 meters back; photos are spectacular. Rubber boots provided if muddy.

Just past El Chato, descend into the lava tunnels. These cavities formed when surface lava cooled while magma flowed beneath, creating passageways stretching hundreds of meters. Bring a headlamp (or use your phone light). The walls show colorful mineral deposits; the acoustics are striking. Mind your head in tight spots.

activities.text: At dusk, head to Puerto Ayora's fish market. Fishermen gut their catch on the dock while pelicans, sea lions, and herons squabble over scraps—hilarious and supremely photogenic. Street kiosks behind the market grill fresh fish daily.

Back in Puerto Ayora by evening, stop at Las Grietas canal. Board the water taxi from the main dock, then walk 10 minutes. It's a volcanic fissure filled with crystalline water between sheer lava cliffs—excellent for easy, shallow snorkeling and swimming. A guide is required.

Galápagos Island Hopping: Santa Cruz, Isabela & San Cristóbal
Galápagos Island Hopping: Santa Cruz, Isabela & San Cristóbal

visits.text: Morning ferry from Isabela to San Cristóbal. Note: there's no direct route. You first ferry to Santa Cruz (2.5 hours), then connect onward to San Cristóbal (another 2 hours). Half your day goes to transport with the stopover in Puerto Ayora. Seasickness medication strongly advised. San Cristóbal is the archipelago's oldest island (2.4 to 4 million years old), where Darwin first set foot in 1835, and happens to be the administrative capital. Puerto Baquerizo Moreno greets you with sea lions sprawled everywhere—on benches, docks, rocks.

The day's highlight: a boat excursion to Kicker Rock (León Dormido), 1.5 hours offshore. This eroded volcanic cone rises 148 meters above water, split by a 20-meter-deep channel. From the north it looks like a shoe (hence 'Kicker'); from the south, a sleeping lion. Snorkeling in the channel ranks among the Galápagos' finest: hammerhead sharks, Galápagos sharks, white-tips, green turtles, eagle rays, tropical fish schools. The currents are strong—experienced swimmers only. Plan 6 hours including boat time, lunch, and a beach break.

Back ashore, visit the Interpretation Center just north of Puerto Baquerizo Moreno. Opened in 1994 with Spanish aid, it charts the Galápagos' natural and human story—from 1535 discovery through penal colonies to Darwin's legacy. Free entry. The center anchors several trails to Cerro Tijeretas and Punta Carola.

Your last dawn in the archipelago—make it count. Depart early on foot from Puerto Baquerizo Moreno toward Cerro Tijeretas (Frigatebird Hill). The 5.5-km loop begins at the Interpretation Center. A paved lava-stone trail climbs through an arid zone thick with cacti; vegetation shifts as you gain altitude. At the summit (roughly 200 meters), panoramic views embrace Wreck Bay, Lobos Island offshore, and Kicker Rock in the distance. This is one of the few places on Earth where both frigatebird species (magnificent and superb) nest in the same colony. You'll also spot a WWII cannon salvaged by Ecuador's navy.

Descending, veer toward Darwin Cove (Muelle Tijeretas)—a free, sheltered snorkeling spot wedged between rocks. Sea lions, sea turtles, marine iguanas, and tropical fish await. Check for territorial males with pups before entering the water.

Continue the trail to Punta Carola, a crescent beach ringed by volcanic formations, 15 minutes' walk from Playa Mann. Pass Darwin's statue—a souvenir photo op. The beach draws surfers (3-meter swells at high tide) and sea lions who colonize it peacefully. If swell is heavy, observe from afar; the surrounding rocks are treacherous.

activities.text: Finish the day at Playa Mann, the nearest beach to town—10 minutes on foot. Fine sand, clear water, and above all: sea lions everywhere, lounging between swimmers with zero concern. At sunset, the bay light is magical.

If your flight departs late, take one final detour to La Lobería, a beach 15 minutes by taxi from town. This is marine iguana country—dozens of them sprawled on black lava rocks, expelling salt through their nostrils. The landscape is untamed and pristine, a perfect summation of Galápagos' magic. Absorb it one last time before heading to San Cristóbal Airport for your return flight to Guayaquil or Quito.

visits.text: Drive from Guayaquil north along the Pacific coast (about 3h). You'll follow the Ruta del Spondylus, the coastal road named after a shell sacred to pre-Columbian civilizations. The landscape shifts dramatically: tropical dry forest, giant cacti, and small fishing villages. Arrive in Puerto López, a quiet town that serves as base for exploring Machalilla National Park.

In the afternoon, head to Los Frailes beach, considered one of Ecuador's most beautiful mainland beaches. Located in Machalilla National Park, it forms a white sand crescent bordered by cliffs and turquoise water. Access is via a 20-minute trail through dry forest (free, registration required at the park entrance). There's no infrastructure on the beach—bring water and a picnic. The calm is total on weekdays.

Full day on Isla de la Plata, nicknamed "the poor man's Galápagos"—a somewhat reductive nickname but it gives the idea. This island located about 40 km offshore from Puerto López hosts colonies of blue-footed boobies, frigatebirds, and albatrosses (April to November for the latter). The boat crossing takes 1h30 and can be rough—take motion sickness medication if you're prone.

On the island, two guided hiking trails (mandatory) of about 2h take you through blue-footed booby nests. These birds have no fear of humans and you can observe them from a few meters away—their mating display, where the male lifts his blue feet one at a time, is hilarious. After the hike, a snorkeling session is included in the excursion: sea turtles, rays, and tropical fish populate the waters around the island.

activities.text: If you're traveling between June and September, watch for humpback whales from Puerto López's waterfront. They migrate each year from Antarctica to breed in the warm waters off Ecuador's coast. Boat tours leave every morning from the port—book the day before. The sight of these 15-meter giants breaching is stunning.

Back at port by mid-afternoon, enjoy Puerto López's waterfront for fresh ceviche prepared by fishermen. The colorful boats on the beach, pelicans circling the stalls—the atmosphere is authentic and relaxed. Pacific sunset guaranteed.

visits.text: Early ferry from Puerto Ayora to Isabela—expect a rough 2.5-hour crossing. Bring seasickness pills. Puerto Villamil welcomes you with a fishing village of 2,200 people, far quieter than Puerto Ayora. Settle in and rent a bike toward the Wall of Tears. The trail hugs the coast for 5 km from town—sand then gravel, about 1 hour by bike.

The Muro de las Lágrimas is a towering wall of volcanic stone, 5 to 7 meters high, 3 meters wide, stretching over 100 meters—built between 1946 and 1959 by prisoners at a penal colony. President Velasco Ibarra established this isolated fortress in 1945 on Isabela, surrounded by 1,000 km of shark-infested ocean. The construction served no purpose except to break prisoners through forced labor. Locals swear it's haunted, hearing wails at dusk. Climb to the overlook—stunning views of Isabela.

On your return, stop at the wetlands to spot the archipelago's largest colony of flamingos—best between 6 and 9 am when they feed. You'll also pass a natural mangrove tunnel sheltering all four endemic mangrove species of the Galápagos.

Isabela's crown jewel awaits. Board your boat for Los Túneles (Cabo Rosa), 1 hour offshore. These submerged lava tunnels formed millions of years ago when lava flows met the ocean. The outer shell solidified while magma continued flowing inside, creating a labyrinth of natural arches, bridges, and basins. Access is strictly controlled—the National Park limits visitors daily. Book with a naturalist guide the day before. It's mandatory.

Snorkeling inside the tunnels is unparalleled. Turquoise, calm water at 2 to 10 meters depth. You'll encounter resting white-tip reef sharks on the sand, enormous green sea turtles (spanning 2 meters), rays (eagle, golden, manta), and if lucky, seahorses—Los Túneles is one of the few places on Earth where they're easily seen. Above water, stand on the lava arches to watch blue-footed boobies perform their courtship dances.

activities.text: Late afternoon: head to Concha de Perla, a tiny natural lagoon accessed via a wooden boardwalk from Puerto Villamil's dock. It's the easiest free snorkeling spot on Isabela—calm, shallow water where sea lions, sea turtles, rays, and tropical fish schools await. No guide required. Rentals available in town for mask and fins.

Afternoon brings the Sierra Negra volcano hike—the only one of Isabela's five volcanoes open to visitors. Its 10-km-wide, 300-meter-deep caldera is the planet's second-largest. The trail covers roughly 16 km round-trip from the trailhead (21 km by taxi from Puerto Villamil), climbing 200 meters over 5 to 6 hours. You ascend through humid forest then suddenly enter a primordial landscape: jet-black lava fields, fumaroles, cinder cones. The 2018 eruption was recent—you'll walk on fresh lava. Pack water, sunscreen, a rain jacket, sturdy shoes. A guide is mandatory. Combining Los Túneles and Sierra Negra in one day is ambitious; both tours start early (6–7 am). If choosing one, Los Túneles is Isabela's unique experience. Plan Sierra Negra for a potential extra day.

visits.text: Start at Plaza Grande, the beating heart of Quito's UNESCO-listed historic center—the very first cultural site inscribed in 1978, alongside Krakow. Surrounding the square: the Palacio de Carondelet (presidential residence since the 16th century), the Metropolitan Cathedral, and the Archbishop's Palace. On Tuesdays at 11am, catch the changing of the guard—it's highly photogenic. Grab a bench, order fresh juice from a street vendor, and watch daily life unfold around the fountain.

Step inside the Iglesia de la Compañía de Jesús, a five-minute walk away. Built between 1605 and 1765 from gray volcanic stone, its gold-leaf interior will leave you speechless—it's South America's finest example of Baroque art. Construction took 160 years, which explains the blend of styles: Mudéjar, Churrigueresque, Neoclassical, and dominant Baroque. The main altarpiece is considered the masterpiece of Quito's colonial art school. Allow a full hour here.

Continue to Plaza de San Francisco and its massive Franciscan convent, founded in 1537 atop the ruins of an Inca palace. With 40,000 m² of buildings—thirteen cloisters, three churches—it's nicknamed the "Escorial of the New World." Inside, over 3,500 works of colonial art and Legarda's famous Winged Virgin (1734) on the main altar. This is the original sculpture whose giant replica stands atop El Panecillo.

Late afternoon, wander down Calle La Ronda, old Quito's most picturesque pedestrian street. Cobblestones, colorful facades, artisan workshops, and cozy cafés line the way. Come in the evening and the vibe shifts: street musicians, open galleries, and the scent of canelazo (hot cinnamon drink spiked with aguardiente). A perfect spot to end the day.

If time allows early or late in the day, make a detour to Mitad del Mundo, 25 km north of Quito. The monument marks the Equator as determined in 1736 by Charles-Marie de La Condamine's expedition. You can plant a foot in each hemisphere—the classic photo op. Right next door, the Inti Ñan ethnographic museum offers fun experiments on the effects of latitude 0° (water flow, balancing an egg). Allow 1.5 hours on-site.

The Basílica del Voto Nacional dominates Quito's skyline—the building rises 115 meters high, with towers exceeding 78 m. It's the largest neo-Gothic basilica in the Americas. French architect Emilio Tarlier drew inspiration from Bourges Cathedral when he drafted plans in 1890, but the first stone wasn't laid until 1892, and construction spanned nearly a century. Fun detail: the gargoyles aren't medieval chimeras but iguanas, tortoises, and armadillos—local fauna. Quiteños say that when the basilica is finally finished, the world will end. Climb the towers—wear good shoes, the final meters involve metal ladders. The view over the historic center is Quito's best.

Take a taxi to El Panecillo, the "little bread loaf" hill rising to 3,016 m. At the summit, the Virgin of Quito—41 meters including the base, assembled from 7,400 aluminum plates by Spanish sculptor Agustín de la Herrán Matorras, installed in 1976. It's the world's tallest aluminum statue, taller than Rio's Christ the Redeemer. And it's the world's only winged Virgin—inspired by a passage from Revelation. The 180° view over Quito is superb. Pro tip: take a taxi up, don't walk—the neighborhood around the stairs isn't safe.

Spectacular climb from Tena back to the highlands via the Papallacta road (3-4h). You ascend from 500 m to over 4,000 m at the pass, then descend to Papallacta at 3,300 m. The landscape shifts from suffocating jungle to wind-swept Andean páramo—a striking contrast in a few hours. Enjoy panoramas over high-altitude lagoons and tall grasses of the páramo before your hot springs stop.

Before driving back to Quito, take the short walk around Papallacta's lagoons in the páramo. The air is crisp, silence total, and tall grasses ripple in the wind. It's an end-of-the-world landscape at 3,500 m, populated by Andean ducks and mountain rabbits. Count 45 minutes for the loop.

activities.text: Stroll through the Rocafuerte neighborhood to sample an almuerzo (daily set menu) and encounter traditional herbalists, chocolatiers, and restorers of religious statues—a living Quito you won't find in guidebooks.

Afternoon at the TelefériQo: this cable car lifts you in 18 minutes from 3,117 m to 3,947 m on the slopes of Pichincha volcano—one of the world's highest gondolas. From Cruz Loma, the view over Quito is dizzying: the city stretches 40 km long but only 10 km wide. On clear days, you'll spot Cotopaxi, Cayambe, and Antisana, all snow-capped. Bring a windbreaker—it's chilly up here. If well-acclimatized, continue on foot to Rucu Pichincha summit (4,696 m, 3h one-way)—the trail is steep and sandy in the final section, but the view from the top sweeps the entire Avenue of Volcanoes.

Relax at Papallacta hot springs, Ecuador's finest. Perched at 3,300 m elevation, the natural hot-water pools (between 36 and 40°C) are outdoors, surrounded by mountains and mist. After 10 days of driving, hiking, and altitude, it's the perfect stop to loosen muscles before the return to Quito (1h30 drive).

visits.text: A driving day along the Avenue of the Volcanoes, the 400-km Andean corridor named by Alexander von Humboldt in 1802. From Quito, you head due south between two rows of volcanoes—Cotopaxi, Tungurahua, Chimborazo loom on the horizon. Take a midway break in Ambato, about 2.5 hours down the road.

Ambato, nicknamed "the city of flowers and fruits," doesn't appear in classic guidebooks but deserves a stop. Founded in the 16th century, it was destroyed three times by earthquakes (1698, 1797, 1949) and rebuilt each time. Stroll around Plaza Montalvo and visit the Casa y Mausoleo de Juan Montalvo—this great Ecuadorian writer died in Paris in 1889, and his embalmed body rests in a Greek-style mausoleum. If you pass through on a Monday, the big market takes over the streets: indigenous people from the Pilahuín communities descend from the mountains to sell their harvests.

Arrive in Riobamba by late afternoon after another 1.5 hours of driving. Perched at 2,750 meters and nicknamed "the Sultana of the Andes," Riobamba sits at the foot of Chimborazo. Take a walk around Plaza Maldonado where the cathedral stands—its facade is one of the rare remnants of the original city, founded in 1534 near Colta lagoon before the 1797 earthquake forced the move.

Head to Chimborazo, 35 minutes from Riobamba. At 6,268 meters, it's Ecuador's highest peak—and more importantly, the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's center, surpassing Everest thanks to the equatorial bulge. The road crosses the wildlife reserve of nearly 60,000 hectares. Keep your eyes open: you'll likely spot vicuñas, wild cousins of the llama reintroduced here in the 1990s. They're not skittish and will lift their heads to study you with curious eyes—but drive slowly, they often cross the road.

Drive up to the Hermanos Carrel refuge at 4,800 meters—accessible without special equipment. From there, a trail leads in 40 minutes to the Edward Whymper refuge at 5,000 meters, named after British alpinist Edward Whymper, already famous for conquering the Matterhorn, who reached this summit on January 4, 1880 with the Carrel brothers. At this altitude, every step weighs heavy: go slowly, hydrate constantly. If the sky clears, the glaciated summit appears above you.

activities.text: Head up to Parque 21 de Abril to see Riobamba with Chimborazo as backdrop—the volcano clears more often late in the day than in the morning. Enjoy the evening with some hornado (roast pork), a Sierra specialty. The small restaurants around Mercado La Merced are the most authentic.

On the way back, stop at the community of La Moya (3,200 m). Their Mountain Museum tells the story of the hieleros, men who climbed Chimborazo to fetch blocks of ice to sell at markets. The last known hielero, Baltazar Ushca, practiced this trade alone for decades. His son-in-law hopes to create a memorial trail in his honor. A shared meal with locals will give you a rare glimpse into Andean life.

Active alternative: agencies in Riobamba offer a mountain bike descent from Carrel refuge (4,800 m) down to San Juan village (3,100 m)—33 km and 1,750 meters of descent through the páramo. Duration about 6 hours, accessible without particular experience.

visits.text: From Baños, continue the descent toward the Amazon heading to Puyo (1h30). You drop even more elevation—heat and humidity rise, vegetation turns dense and tropical. Make a stop at Mirador Indichuris, 45 minutes south of Puyo: perched at 1,000 m, this viewpoint run by the indigenous Indichuris community ("children of the sun" in Quechua) offers panoramic views over the confluence of the Puyo and Pastaza rivers and the endless Amazon canopy. There are also caves adorned with carved faces and a swing over the abyss.

Don't leave without visiting Paseo de los Monos, a nonprofit refuge tucked deep in the rainforest. Volunteers—sometimes French-speaking—guide you among monkeys, coatis, parrots, and tortoises rescued after illegal trafficking seizures. Some animals, too habituated to humans or injured, can never return to the wild. The place is moving and the welcome very warm.

activities.text: Canoe excursion on Río Puyo or Río Napo to reach a Kichwa Amazonian community. You'll be welcomed with traditional achiote body paint (red plant pigment), can join ritual dances, and discover the use of jungle medicinal plants. It's a brief but authentic immersion into the culture of the Oriente peoples.
